newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritanians slow to vote in parliamentary poll.
newsitem.headline: Mauritanians slow to vote in parliamentary poll.

text.p: Nicholas Phythian

Mauritanians voted for a new national assembly on Friday in a major test of the West African nation's fledgling democracy but even with opposition candidates standing for the first time turnout appeared low.

Opposition supporters, many of whom expressed irritation at the heavy turnout of soldiers and other members of the security forces at polling stations, said problems over voting cards prevented many people voting. Many cried fraud.
"We have a large number of our militants who could not vote," Saad Ibrahima, general secretary of the radical Action for Change Party, told reporters.
Almost half the 2.2 million people in the impoverished mainly Moslem nation at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert are eligible to vote.

Dominant light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population in the former French colony which won independence in 1960 and straddles black and Arab Africa. Arabic-speaking ex-slaves make up the remainder.
"The big irregularity that we noticed was that they are all black Africans who could not vote," Saad said.
Poll organisers and officials acknowledged problems with voting cards -- mistyped names or identity card numbers.
But returning officers and supporters of President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya and the ruling Democratic Social and Republican Party blamed administrative inadequacies.
"It's a problem for everyone," Taya supporter Bilal Saleh said at one town hall where dozens of voters with card problems waited for special papers from officials allowing them to vote.
Polling in Nouakchott, the dusty capital, was slow and turnout in many stations two hours from the 7 p.m. close was as low as 20 to 25 percent.
It was not immediately clear how the poll was going in the interior of the sparsely population country.
Voters -- the men in blue or white robes, the women in brightly coloured muslin -- squatted in the sand, waiting patiently in separate queues early in the day.
Soldiers and security forces guarded polling stations, checking voters' credentials before allowing them in.

The opposition, which boycotted the 1992 poll denouncing irregularities, is hoping to make its mark ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998. It has accused the authorities of censorship, denying it a fair hearing this time.
The Union of Democratic Forces-New Era, Action for Change and the Union for Democracy and Progress are the three main opposition parties
Taya and the ruling party emerged victorious from 1992 elections that launched Mauritania's multi-party experiment. The ruling party won 67 of the assembly's 79 seats.
Taya, a French-trained army colonel, seized power in a bloodless coup in 1984. He launched the democratic transition in 1991 and won a six-year term as president a year later.
Thirteen political parties have put up candidates for Friday's poll along with more than 50 independents -- mostly disgruntled ruling party members passed over for the poll.
Women are also standing for the first time. Most of the 26 women candidates are from the ruling party.
First results are expected on Friday night but the final results could take a couple of days to emerge. Second-round run- offs are planned for October 18.
